newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's first independent TV network planned.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's first independent TV network planned.

text.p: Journalists fed up with a censored diet of state-run television said on Sunday they were setting up Croatia's first independent television network to liberalise a media scene dominated by the ruling nationalists.
The co-editors of the new enterprise resigned from state television (HRT) after its managers axed their popular late-night show, which featured uncut foreign news footage about Croatia.

The simply-named "TV Network", whose news show would be modelled on the U.S.-based Cable News Network (CNN), should open on December 1, editor-in-chief-to-be Denis Latin told the state-run Zagreb newspaper Vecernji List.

It would link up several local, youth-oriented independent stations in major cities across the former Yugoslav republic and would offer a mix of news and entertainment for seven hours a day to start, he said.
It was unclear if TV Network would seek a national broadcasting license or opt, at least initially, for a more modest scheme in which stations would pool programming.

Powerful rightists in Croatia's ruling party are hostile to independent media and could obstruct the rise of critical TV news at a time of sagging government popularity ahead of presidential elections next year.
But analysts said TV Network's prospects would be improved by the reported financial stake of Miroslav Kutle, a property magnate with blue-chip connections to President Franjo Tudjman's government.

The government has muzzled some media foes through forced buyouts and hounded others with punitive taxes and lawsuits. But authorities are now under pressure to ease media repression to strengthen Croatia's relationship with the European Union.
Judging by a spate of generally neutral articles about the project in the state-run media, the authorities appear to be taking TV Network seriously.
"The latest events, which have seen some of HRT's biggest stars crossing over to TV Network, have set tongues wagging," said the government-controlled Zagreb newspaper Vjesnik.

Media sources said Silvana Mendjusic, an HRT correspondent who was given an award by Tudjman for her reporting of the war with rebel minority Serbs, had quit to joint TV Network and other HRT journalists might also defect.
"We're negotiating with a number of people but only those who share our views on TV. We want to introduce a modern style of reporting," Latin said.

"There will be no standard of 'appropriateness', either for our journalists or the news," he added, using the euphemism for subservience to state authority that guided television under Yugoslav communist rule and prevails in independent Croatia.

TV Network is to be jointly financed by Kutle and Nino Pavic, an independent media entrepreneur who owns Globus, a leading weekly that has exposed alleged corruption and racketeering by figures linked to the ruling party.
Pavic also plans to start publishing the Croatian version of Playboy magazine soon.
